inline.s: There is yet another kind of person who twists the saying “Originally a Buddha, not belonging to cultivation and realization.” He says that it is originally complete and need not be cultivated or realized, and all day long he is listless and scattered, indulging his feelings and giving free rein. Wasting his time, he still calls himself “an extraordinary man, free and at ease amid conditions.” Such a person is going to suffer bitter consequences.
One who has some mind of the Way, again, cannot find a place to start.

Or there be one who is afraid of idle thoughts, and can neither get rid of them; all day long vexed and troubled, blaming himself for his heavy karmic obstructions, he thereby loses the mind of the Way.

Or there be one who wants to fight to the death with idle thoughts, angrily clenching his fists and puffing up his breath, sticking out his chest and staring wide-eyed, as if in earnest, about to wage a war to the death with idle thoughts; little does he know that idle thoughts cannot be fought to the death, and that instead he will end up spewing blood and going mad.
Or there be one who fears falling into emptiness; little does he know that a “ghost” has already been born, that the emptiness cannot be emptied away and enlightenment cannot be attained.
Or there be one who uses the mind to seek enlightenment; little does he know that seeking to enlighten and wishing to become a Buddha are all a great idle thought. Sand is not the basis of rice
(boiling sand cannot make rice)
; seek until the “year of the donkey,” and one will certainly never attain enlightenment.

Or there be one who, hitting upon a stick or two of quiet incense, gives rise to a feeling of joy. That is merely the blind-eyed turtle praising a hole in a log—happening upon it by chance, not genuine practice; and it is an extra layer of the obstruction of joy.
[A stick or two of quiet incense]During that stick or two of incense, the mind is pure, clear, and still.
Or there be one who in stillness feels pure, clear, and comfortable, but in activity cannot manage; so he flees noise for stillness and sits in dead water, passing his days.
Such cases are many, very many.
For the beginner who cannot find the path, it is truly difficult: with awareness but without illumination, one is scattered and cannot “settle into the hall”
(for the mind is scattered and the effort cannot come to rest in the hall)
; with illumination but without awareness, one again sits soaked and drowned in dead water.

Though applying effort is said to be difficult, once one finds the path it is quite easy. What is the easiness of the beginner’s effort? There is no cleverness to it—just let go. Let go of what? Just let go of all ignorance and affliction.

Fellow practitioners all! This body of ours, when one breath does not come, is a corpse. The reason we cannot let go is only that we value it heavily; hence self and other, right and wrong, love and hate, grasping and rejecting arise. If one were certain that this body is a corpse, not treasuring it, and not regarding it as “I” in the least, what would there be to let go of?

Provided one can let go, then at all times and in all places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, in activity or stillness, busy or free, the whole body within and without is cold and still, only a single thought of doubt, peacefully and continuously doubting on, without the slightest admixture of another thought. A single huatou is like a great sword leaning against the sky; whoever touches its blade has his traces wiped out and his voice silenced. What idle thoughts are there to fear? What idle fellow can strike you? Who goes to distinguish activity from stillness? Who has recourse to existence or emptiness?

If one fears idle thoughts, that adds one more layer of idle thought; if one is aware of being pure and clear, it has long since ceased to be pure and clear; if one fears falling into emptiness, one has already sunk into existence; if one wishes to become a Buddha, one has already entered the demonic path.
Therefore, so long as one recognizes the path
(the path is this single thought of letting everything go and single-mindedly raising the huatou)

, then carrying water and hauling firewood are none other than the wondrous Way, and hoeing the fields and planting the soil are always the living meaning of Chan. It is not only by sitting cross-legged in meditation all day that one is counted as applying effort in the cultivation of the Way.
